summary: Learners read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation and show them on analogue clocks. Core rules: for p.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59, add 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 onward, subtract 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (never 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The decisive step is deciding FIRST whether a time is before or after noon — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps where learners wrongly apply the rule.
misconceptions: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
Adds 12 to a.m. times too (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38')
When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m. on the answer

activities.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
steps: Move a marker along a day-line running from midnight 00:00 through noon 12:00 and back to midnight, watching a 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) readout and a 24-hour readout change together as the marker moves.

Stop the marker just before noon and just after: just before, both displays read 11:59 (11:59 a.m. and 11:59); at noon both read 12:00 and only the 12-hour LABEL flips from a.m. to p.m. (so it shows 12:00 p.m., not 1:00). Then move on past 1 p.m. and watch the 24-hour clock tick to 13:00 while the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. — this is where the 12-of-difference first appears.
Stop at midnight and read both displays; confirm the 24-hour clock shows 00:00 (a new day starting), not 24:00, by looking at what it shows one minute before and one minute after.

For a chosen afternoon time from 1 p.m. onward, read the 12-hour value, then the 24-hour value, and state the relationship: 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' — noting that the 12:xx noon hour is the exception, where both forms still read 12.

If a day-line is available, use its paired displays and boundary labels at 00:00 (midnight, new day) and 12:00 (noon); if not, draw the day-line on paper, mark 00:00, 12:00 and 24:00->00:00, and write both forms side by side for several times.
activities.insight: The +12 / -12 relationship is not an arbitrary rule but the afternoon and evening hours continuing to count on past 12; noon and midnight are fixed boundaries, the 12:xx noon hour still reads 12 in both forms, and the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 straight to 00:00.

activities.title: Decide before-or-after-noon first, then convert
steps: For each time given, first state whether it is before noon (a.m.), after noon (p.m.), or a boundary (midnight/noon), BEFORE doing any arithmetic.
Convert 3:45 p.m. to 24-hour time (expected 15:45, add 12) and 9:45 a.m. to 24-hour time (expected 09:45 — add a leading zero, do NOT add 12).
Convert 19:30 to 12-hour time (expected 7:30 p.m., subtract 12) and 12:20 to 12-hour time (expected 12:20 p.m. — stays the same, do NOT subtract).
Write midnight and noon in 24-hour time (midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00).
Write a single-digit-hour time such as 6:38 a.m. in 24-hour form and check it has exactly four digits (06:38).
Always label a.m. or p.m. when writing a 12-hour answer.
activities.insight: Whether to add or subtract 12 depends on deciding first if the time is before or after noon; a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 keep their hour (single-digit hours gain a leading zero), p.m. times from 1:00 get +12, 24-hour times from 13:00 get -12, and the 12:xx noon hour, the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (written 00:xx) and the midnight/noon boundaries are exceptions handled by inspection, not arithmetic.

activities.title: Match and build a conversion table
steps: Match a mixed set of 12-hour times (with a.m./p.m.) to their 24-hour equivalents, including at least one morning time, one 12:xx p.m. time, and a midnight item.
Build or complete a two-column table pairing each 12-hour time with its 24-hour form, filling the missing cell in whichever direction is blank.

For a pair you matched, state in words what is the same and what is different between the two forms (same minutes; hour differs by 12 from 1 p.m. onward and in the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour, which is written 00:xx; 24-hour has four digits).

Choose correctly between a tempting wrong answer and the right one, e.g. for '6 p.m. in 24-hour time' decide between 16:00 (a +10 slip) and 18:00, and for midnight decide between 24:00 and 00:00, explaining why the wrong one is wrong.
Represent one converted time on an analogue clock to connect the notation to the clock face.
activities.insight: Seeing the two notations paired across many times — and articulating what stays the same (minutes) and what changes (the hour, from 1 p.m. onward, plus the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour becoming 00:xx) — consolidates the rule and exposes the specific slips (+10, adding 12 to a.m., 24:00, dropping a.m./p.m.).

activities.title: Timetable word problems that force the right decision
steps: Read short timetable or schedule problems (e.g. a train leaves at 15:45 — what time is that in the afternoon? A film starts at 9:45 a.m. — write its 24-hour time) and convert as needed to answer.
For each problem, say whether the time is before or after noon before converting, then give the answer in the format the question asks for, labelling a.m./p.m. when giving 12-hour times.
Include at least one morning time, one noon-hour (12:xx) time, and one midnight/noon reference so the morning and noon traps appear in context.
Explain your answer to a partner or in writing, justifying why you added, subtracted, or left the hour unchanged.
activities.insight: The conversion rule is applied to solve real timetable questions, and the before/after-noon check and the boundary exceptions still govern whether to add, subtract, or leave the hour alone.

checkQuestion: Set conversions in BOTH directions and WATCH the method: (1) 'Write 3:45 p.m. as a 24-hour time', then 'Write 9:45 a.m. as a 24-hour time.' (2) 'Read 19:30 — what is that in 12-hour time?', then 'What about 12:20?' (3) 'How do you write midnight, and noon, in 24-hour time?' Watch whether they add exactly 12 to p.m. (but not a.m.), use a leading zero, subtract 12 only from 13:00 onwards, keep a.m./p.m. on the answer, and handle midnight and noon.
